question: Can model scale, gradient-descent training time, and data volume be described through one dynamical scaling variable that also explains model-, epoch-, and sample-wise double descent?

key_findings.claim: In the paper's random-subspace model, function-space dynamics converge to a trajectory indexed by the product of controllable parameter dimension and time.
key_findings.evidence: With unit-Gaussian subspace matrix R, KRR^T K^T concentrates around pKK^T. Theorem 1 bounds the deviation from the deterministic gradient-flow trajectory A_{pt}; the bound improves with p at fixed pt but worsens exponentially along long trajectories.

key_findings.claim: CNN and MLP experiments show approximate inverse tradeoffs between a chosen effective scale and SGD epochs needed to cross one generalization threshold.
key_findings.evidence: Across MNIST, CIFAR-10, and SVHN, widths 1-100 and several sample counts produce roughly parallel log-log curves near the claimed one-to-one slope. Scale is not raw parameters: it is set to the cube root of parameter count using Appendix B's heuristic.

key_findings.claim: Small/long and large/short runs predict each other's MNIST loss trajectories qualitatively under the pt substitution.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 3 maps a small model trained up to 100 epochs to larger-model scale and maps varied models trained for one epoch to a medium model's later epochs. Curves are close around onset of generalization, with visible discrepancies that the authors say may need task-specific calibration.

anchors.section: 4 Predicting Optimal Network Scale and Training Time

key_findings.claim: The proposed unified error expression combines spectral signal/noise learning with the pt substitution and can represent several double-descent shapes.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 9 decomposes linear-regression test error into decaying signal and growing noise components at singular-value-specific rates. Equation 10 replaces time by pt and lets the singular spectrum depend on sample count, yielding qualitatively different shapes depending on when noise and signal modes are acquired.

key_findings.claim: The experiments reproduce reduced sample requirements at larger width and persistent label-noise penalties over epochs and scale.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 5, 6, and 9 show larger selected models crossing the MSE threshold with fewer samples and 20% corrupted labels raising error broadly over time/scale while having more localized effects over sample count. Some CIFAR-10 and SVHN curves turn upward at large scale.

key_findings.claim: The theorem's equivalence is largely a parameterization result and does not establish equivalence for ordinary neural-network scaling.
key_findings.evidence: Its unit-variance extra columns increase KR R^T K^T linearly with p at fixed learning rate, so width acts like learning-rate multiplication. The authors acknowledge that NTK parameterization changes the result. Real narrower networks are not random linear subspaces of a shared low-rank function model, and feature dimension r is fixed below every p.

key_findings.claim: The effective-scale exponent is selected by an unvalidated heuristic that helps define the empirical equivalence being tested.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix B assumes an m-wide network is an ensemble of O(m^2) independent submodels, infers MSE O(1/m^2), and combines this with a capacity-counting argument to set p to the cube root of raw parameter count. The interpolation threshold is not measured directly, and alternate exponents or out-of-sample slope error are not compared.

key_findings.claim: The label-noise evidence is internally disconnected from the claimed equivalence because those experiments use Adam, for which the paper's own scale-time test fails.
key_findings.evidence: Section 3.2 says Adam's epoch-to-scale curve first falls then rises and limits the result to gradient descent. Appendix C.4 states that the noise and loss-shape experiments use Adam, yet Sections 5.4-5.5 interpret them through Equation 10's pt equivalence without deriving an Adam analogue.

key_findings.claim: Equation 10 is an expressive explanatory family, not a fitted, identified, or prospectively validated scaling law.
key_findings.evidence: The infinitely many signal coefficients, noise coefficients, singular values, and their sample dependence are left unspecified; no fit, likelihood, held-out extrapolation error, uncertainty interval, or baseline comparison is reported. The predictive experiment instead copies one empirical trajectory using pt.

method.core_idea: Model width as the dimension of a random trainable subspace whose gradient-flow speed grows linearly with dimension, then substitute the resulting scale-time product into a spectral signal/noise model of generalization.
method.mechanism: Prove concentration of a random subspace kernel around p times a fixed kernel; define an empirical effective scale from a heuristic exponent; test iso-performance scale/epoch curves; transfer loss curves along constant pt; and use singular-mode learning rates to explain nonmonotonic error over time, scale, and samples.
assumptions: The task function depends only on a fixed low-dimensional linear projection of parameters.
Smaller models behave like unit-Gaussian random subspaces of a shared larger model.
Gradient flow with a width-independent parameterization approximates SGD-trained networks.
The cube root of raw parameter count is a valid effective scale across tested MLPs and CNNs.
Signal and label-noise modes are separable and learned at singular-value-specific rates.
A result shown for SGD can explain Adam experiments despite the observed non-equivalence under Adam.

techniques.role: Makes model dimension multiply the effective function-space gradient-flow rate.
Transfers an empirical loss trajectory between model sizes and epoch counts.
Separates decaying signal error from growing noise-fit error by data singular mode.
Measures iso-performance epochs across widths and dataset sizes.
Contrasts clean and 20%-corrupted labels over time, scale, and sample count.

evaluations.setting: Linear random-subspace regression over five trials
evaluations.metric: Iterations needed to reach fixed loss at varying controllable dimension
evaluations.result: Iso-loss curves approximately follow inverse one-to-one scale/time proportionality.
evaluations.baseline: The exact pt prediction from the theorem's noise-free trajectory.

evaluations.setting: Six-layer MLPs and CNNs on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and SVHN with SGD
evaluations.metric: Epochs required for test MSE below 0.09 across widths, samples, and five seeds
evaluations.result: Curves are broadly consistent with inverse effective-scale/time tradeoffs, with visible task/model deviations.
evaluations.baseline: A fixed -1 log-log slope after defining scale as parameter_count^(1/3).

evaluations.metric: Visual agreement of predicted and true train/test MSE curves
evaluations.result: Transferred curves track the broad transition but no aggregate forecast error or held-out calibration score is reported.

evaluations.setting: Vision networks with clean or 20% corrupted labels, primarily using Adam
evaluations.metric: Test MSE versus epochs, chosen effective scale, and sample count
evaluations.result: Noise penalties persist over epochs/scale and some large-scale curves are U-shaped; sample-wise effects often shrink at high data volume.

limitations: The neural-network claim is not a consequence of the random-subspace theorem.
Empirical scale uses a heuristic exponent without model selection or sensitivity analysis.
Adam violates the measured equivalence but is used for key claimed consequences.
The unified law leaves its spectral coefficients and sample dependence unidentified.
Forecast quality is shown visually without quantitative extrapolation metrics or uncertainty calibration.
Experiments use small vision networks, MSE classification, 100 epochs, and one performance threshold.
The LLM accessibility claim is not tested on language models, repeated-token regimes, or downstream tasks.
Compute, memory, optimizer tuning, batch scaling, and inference costs are not included in the equivalence.
failure_modes: Changing width parameterization or learning-rate scaling removes the apparent p-fold speedup.
Feature learning gives different-size networks different trajectories rather than different speeds on one path.
A small model lacks a representation that extra epochs cannot create.
Repeated data eventually overfits or yields vanishing returns even when pt is constant.
An adaptive optimizer changes its effective rate nonmonotonically with width.
The chosen cube-root transform can make unrelated curves appear parallel.
Flexible spectral coefficients explain observed curves post hoc but fail prospective scale forecasts.
The generalization threshold changes the measured slope or ranking.
reusable_insights: Treat training duration as a first-class scaling variable and measure full loss surfaces, not final checkpoints alone.
Separate same-trajectory speedup from genuinely new representation capacity.
Report scaling laws under explicit parameterization, optimizer, batch, and learning-rate conventions.
Validate an effective-size definition independently before using it to demonstrate a scaling relation.
Use held-out scale regimes and forecast scores to distinguish prediction from qualitative explanation.
Probe clean and noisy spectral modes to understand nonmonotonic training dynamics.
open_questions: What scale-time relation remains after matching neural tangent kernels and effective learning rates across widths?
Can effective dimension be measured prospectively from Jacobians or interpolation capacity rather than fitted curve shape?
Does any calibrated equivalence hold for AdamW transformers over multiple orders of model and token scale?
When do extra parameters alter the learned feature basis so that time cannot substitute for scale?
Can Equation 10 be made identifiable and beat simpler broken-power-law forecasts on held-out scales?
How do data repetition, batch size, schedules, and optimizer state enter a compute-normalized law?
What are the uncertainty bounds when extrapolating far beyond the observed scale/time rectangle?

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Double Descent: Where Bigger Models and More Data Hurt
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct predecessor unifying epoch-, model-, and sample-wise double descent.
competitive_landscape.difference: Nakkiran et al. define effective model complexity and empirically conjecture generalized double descent. The reviewed paper proposes a specific pt dynamics and signal/noise account for why scale and epochs may share a curve.

competitive_landscape.title: Broken Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.difference: Caballero et al. fit and score smoothly broken power laws across many architectures/tasks, including double descent. The reviewed paper offers a dynamical mechanism but does not fit or benchmark its unified spectral form.

competitive_landscape.title: Revisiting Neural Scaling Laws in Language and Vision
competitive_landscape.difference: Alabdulmohsin et al. choose laws by held-out extrapolation loss over 90 tasks and give a reliable fitting recipe. The reviewed work transfers curves through pt but omits an equivalent quantitative forecast audit.

competitive_landscape.title: A Dynamical Model of Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.difference: Bordelon, Atanasov, and Pehlevan predict different rather than equal time and width exponents, asymmetric compute-optimal allocation, and data-reuse gaps in a solvable random-feature model. This directly challenges universal pt equivalence.

competitive_landscape.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Hoffmann et al. fit more than 400 language-model runs up to 16B parameters/500B tokens and validate a compute-optimal smaller model on downstream tasks. The reviewed paper tests far smaller vision models and treats epochs, not mostly unique token count, as time.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Muennighoff et al. vary repetition in 400 runs up to 9B parameters and 900B tokens, finding about four repeats nearly harmless but diminishing value thereafter. This supplies the language/data-reuse boundary missing from a simple pt substitution.

competitive_landscape.title: Resolving Discrepancies in Compute-Optimal Scaling of Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Porian et al. show last-layer cost, warmup, and scale-dependent optimizer tuning explain conflicting compute-optimal laws. Their findings underscore that optimizer and schedule controls cannot be abstracted into model scale alone.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Model size and training time are proportionally interchangeable, enabling cross-scale prediction and a single theory of model-, epoch-, and sample-wise double descent.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The random-subspace concentration result cleanly demonstrates one setting where dimension rescales gradient-flow time, and the vision surfaces motivate measuring duration jointly with scale. Effective complexity, time-wise double descent, flexible nonmonotonic laws, and dynamical scaling theories already exist. The chosen empirical scale, optimizer mismatch, and unfitted Equation 10 substantially narrow the general claim.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Novelty is moderate as a sharp hypothesis and experimental lens, but evidence does not support a unified law for ordinary neural networks or LLMs. The publishable core is a parameterization-conditional random-subspace theorem plus a benchmarkable conjecture.

reviewer_notes: Read all 22 pages, theorem proof, effective-parameter heuristic, experimental protocol, and all supplementary plots. Visually inspected scale-time surfaces, transfer curves, and the full noise grid on pages 5, 6, 9, and 21. Audited the SGD/Adam mismatch and checked primary arXiv records for double descent, broken laws, dynamical laws, compute-optimal training, repeated-data scaling, and optimizer-confound work through 2026-08-23.
